newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Basics of EU stability pact set, but detail lacking.
newsitem.headline: Basics of EU stability pact set, but detail lacking.

text.p: Europe's top financial officials this weekend cleared key hurdles in their quest for a stability pact to control public spending once countries enter monetary union, but failed to agree exactly how the deal will work.

European Union finance ministers and central bank governors said at the end of informal one-day talks in Dublin, Ireland, on Saturday the broad outline of plans to punish governments that exceeded certain budget deficit limits were now in place.
But specifics of the plan -- including the size of fines to be levied on offenders -- were referred to committees in the hope a consensus could be thrashed out by the end of the year.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, the architect of the plans to ensure fiscal discipline within Europe's monetary union -- set to start on January 1, 1999 -- said he was satisfied with progress although issues remained unresolved.
After the meeting Waigel said, "I am satisfied. We are following exactly on the road we started on one year ago."

The German minister initially proposed the concept of a stability pact as a means of ensuring that countries which pass the economic test set for entry to the single currency do not later become lax in their fiscal policies.

The entry criteria for EMU laid down in the Maastricht Treaty require countries which want to meld their currencies into the Euro to meet targets on interest and exchange rates, inflation, budget deficits and public borrowing.

The budgetary goals -- which call for annual deficits to total no more than three percent of gross domestic product and total debt of no more than 60 percent of GDP -- have proved by far the hardest for most countries to meet.

This, combined with the fact that their fate on all the other criteria will be inextricably intertwined once the Euro has been established, meant there was a particular need for wideranging agreement on fiscal issues.

European Union commissioner Yves Thibault de Silguy echoed the views of many officials by saying this weekend that the planned stability pact was essential for the credibility of the new Euro in financial markets and with the general public.
Without such a pact, overspending by one Euro member state could undermine the stability of the currency by driving up interest rates and damaging market trust in the Euro.

Under the terms of the pact agreed in Dublin, countries will face sanctions if they notch up a deficit exceeding three percent of Gross Domestic Product unless they take immediate corrective action or face exceptional circumstances.

French central bank governor Jean-Claude Trichet told reporters EU financial officials had agreed four key elements which would smooth the decision-making process and lay down clear rules on what delinquent countries could expect.
Trichet said it had been agreed that the "exceptional and temporary circumstances" under which a country could exceed the three percent level without sanctions must be predefined.

If these did not apply sanctions would always be levied and this would take the form of an interest-free deposit. Finally, if no action was taken, this deposit would be converted into a non-refundable fine.
Ministers also said there was consensus, but not unanimous approval, on the idea that sanctions should be imposed within a calendar year of an excessive deficit being recorded.
Countries would be expected to draw up their accounts for a year by the following March, and implement corrective action before the year-end, to avoid sanctions kicking in.

But there was no consensus on the detail needed to flesh out the skeleton framework, leaving working parties with a large area of ground to cover by December, when ministers hope a complete pact will be ratified by a summit meeting.

Officials said a German proposal calling for a deposit of 0.25 percent of GDP for each percentage point of excessive deficit was still on the table alongside a European Commission proposal for a smaller deposit per percentage point, capped at a maximum of 0.5 percent.
"The type and size of (the deposits) has yet to be agreed," Waigel said.

There was also no agreement on the precise definitions of exceptional circumstances -- an issue Germany sees as essential if the pact is to be applied swiftly and at least semi-automatically once a budget is exceeded.
